newsitem.title: USA: PIXAR likely to produce "Toy Story" video sequel.
newsitem.headline: PIXAR likely to produce "Toy Story" video sequel.

text.p: PIXAR Animation Studios Inc has all but decided to produce a home video sequel to its award winning "Toy Story" computer animated film and release it in 1998, its chief financial officer said.

"We've done a lot of thinking and exploring about a video sequel but we have not gotten to the point of a green light yet," Lawrence Levy, chief financial officer, told the Robertson, Stephens & Co technology conference. He said PIXAR has already invested money in the idea.
"If we did it, we would want to get it out in 1998," he added.

"Toy Story" was the first feature length animated film ever to be produced entirely by computer. It was a box office hit in 1995 and 1996 and to date has grossed $350 million in box office revenues. It was released by the Walt Disney Co, which issued a home video sequel to its animated film hit "Aladdin."
Earlier this week, PIXAR and Disney announced a change in the structure of their film production and distribution relationship which promises to be much more profitable for PIXAR.
"It changes completely the economics of PIXAR's future," Levy said Wednesday.

In sum, Disney and PIXAR signed a deal to jointly produce five computer animated films. PIXAR and Disney will share evenly the film production costs while Disney will bear the marketing and distribution costs alone. When a film produces revenues, Disney will recoup its marketing and distribution investment and then the remaining revenues will be split evenly between the two companies. By contrast, PIXAR got 10 percent of the profits generated by "Toy Story," Levy said.
Robertson, Stephens analyst Keith Benjamin said he expects to "significantly increase" his estimates of PIXAR's earnings for 1998 and beyond because of the new deal.
Levy said it won't be until 1999 when the full impact of the economic benefits of the deal show up in PIXAR's financial statements.
Levy also countered rumors that PIXAR chief executive officer Steve Jobs is spending most of his time these days at Apple Computer Inc, which he recently rejoined in a top advisory post.

"I think Apple investors should be concerned that Steve is spending too much time at PIXAR," rather than the other way around, Levy said. The time he spends at Apple "is down to about four hours a week now," he said.
